items.prompt: Should pupils be allowed to bring mobile phones to school? Write a balanced argument with points for and against, and a conclusion.

criteria.label: The introduction states the question clearly
Gives points for and against, each with a reason or example
Uses linking phrases such as however, on the other hand and on balance
Uses a formal, impersonal style
The conclusion weighs up both sides and gives a view
Spelling, grammar and punctuation are accurate

planning: How will your introduction state the question?
What are two or three points for, with evidence or examples?
What are two or three points against, with evidence or examples?
Which side is stronger in your conclusion, and why?
items.model:
Should Pupils Bring Mobile Phones to School?

Many families now give their children mobile phones. Should pupils be allowed to bring them to school?

Supporters argue that phones help keep children safe, because parents can contact them on the way home. Phones can also be useful for learning, for example to record a science experiment.

On the other hand, phones can distract pupils during lessons. Some people also worry that expensive phones could be lost or damaged.

On balance, I believe pupils should be allowed to bring phones, as long as they are switched off and kept in a locker until the end of the day. This keeps the safety benefit without the distraction.
hints: Keep your own opinion until the conclusion.
Use a new paragraph for each side of the argument.
Phrases such as some people believe help you sound fair.
items.explanation: A balanced argument presents both sides fairly, with evidence, before giving a conclusion.

items.prompt: Write a formal letter to your town council asking for a pedestrian crossing near your school. Explain the problem and suggest a solution.

criteria.label: Uses formal letter layout with a suitable greeting and sign-off
Explains the problem clearly, with evidence
Makes a clear, polite request
Uses formal vocabulary and avoids contractions
Organises ideas into paragraphs
Spelling and punctuation are accurate

planning: What is the problem, and where exactly is it?
What evidence can you give, such as how busy the road is?
What exactly do you want the council to do?
How will you end politely and formally?
items.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing on behalf of the pupils of SD Mekar Sari to request a pedestrian crossing on Jalan Diponegoro, outside our school gate.

Every morning, more than 300 pupils cross this road. During a survey last week, our class counted an average of 42 vehicles passing the gate every five minutes between 6.30 and 7.00. Many drivers do not slow down, and younger pupils often wait several minutes before it is safe to cross.

A zebra crossing with flashing lights would warn drivers and allow pupils to cross safely.

I would be grateful if the council could consider this request at its next meeting.

Yours faithfully,

Annisa Rahma, School Council
hints: Give real details: the name of the road, the time of day and what you have seen.
Remember: Dear Sir or Madam goes with Yours faithfully.
items.explanation: A formal letter of request explains a problem with evidence, makes a clear request and keeps a polite, formal tone.

items.prompt: Write an explanation of a natural process, such as the water cycle or how a seed grows. Use a title, subheadings and cause and effect connectives.

criteria.label: Has a title, an introduction and subheadings
Explains each stage in a logical order
Uses cause and effect connectives such as consequently and as a result
Uses and explains technical words
Uses the present tense and a formal style
Spelling and punctuation are accurate

planning: Which process will you explain, and what happens first?
Which subheadings will split the explanation into stages?
Which technical words will you use, and how will you explain them?
Which connectives will show cause and effect?
items.model:
How a Seed Becomes a Plant

A seed contains a tiny young plant and a store of food. With the right conditions, it grows into a new plant.

Waking up
When a seed takes in water, its coat softens and splits. This stage is called germination, and it also needs warmth and air.

Roots and shoots
First, a root grows downwards to anchor the seedling and take in water. Next, a shoot grows upwards towards the light.

Making food
Once the first leaves open, the plant makes its own food using light, water and carbon dioxide from the air. As a result, it no longer needs the food stored in the seed.
hints: Subheadings help the reader find each stage of the process.
Explain each technical word the first time you use it.
items.explanation: An explanation describes how or why something happens, stage by stage, using technical words and cause and effect connectives.

items.prompt: Write a biography of someone who has made a difference to their community, or of a famous Indonesian. Use paragraphs in time order.

criteria.label: Uses the third person and the past tense consistently
Events are in clear time order, with dates or time phrases
Each paragraph covers one stage of the person’s life
Includes specific facts and achievements
Ends by explaining why the person matters
Spelling, grammar and punctuation are accurate

planning: What are the key dates and events in the person’s life?
What problems did they face, and how did they deal with them?
What are they remembered for?
How will your last paragraph show why they matter today?
items.model:
Wati Susanti was born in 1975 in a small fishing village near Gresik. Her parents could not afford many books, so she read old newspapers that her father brought home from the market.

After finishing secondary school, she trained as a teacher in Surabaya. In 2001, she returned to her village and found that the children there had no library at all.

In 2003, she turned the front room of her house into a reading corner with forty donated books. Within ten years, it had grown into a community library with more than 5,000 books and weekly story sessions.

Today, her library still opens every afternoon, and several of the children who once read in her front room have become teachers themselves.
hints: Collect the key dates and events first, and put them in order.
Include at least one difficulty the person faced and how they dealt with it.
items.explanation: A biography tells the story of a real person’s life in time order, using facts, dates and the third person, and shows why the person matters.

items.prompt: Write a story that begins on the morning of a competition. Flash back to how the main character prepared, then return to the competition for the ending.

criteria.label: Opens with an engaging scene on the day of the competition
Uses a clear flashback, signalled with time phrases or had
Returns smoothly to the present for the ending
Shows feelings through actions, dialogue and figurative language
Uses paragraphs and punctuates dialogue correctly

planning: What is the competition, and how does your character feel that morning?
Which memory will your flashback show?
How will you signal the jump back and the return to the present?
What happens in the end, and what has your character learned?
items.model:
The starting pistol was in the referee’s hand, and Dani’s legs felt like jelly.

Three months earlier, he had stood on the same track, gasping, while the others finished a whole lap ahead. That night, Kakek had handed him a battered stopwatch. “Every morning before school,” he had said. “Just you and the clock.”

So every morning, while the street was still grey and quiet, Dani had run. Some days he had beaten the clock. Most days he had not.

Bang!

Dani flew. By the last bend, he could hear only his own breathing. He came third, but he crossed the line four seconds faster than ever before.

In the crowd, Kakek held up the stopwatch and grinned.
hints: Use a time phrase such as Three months earlier to start the flashback.
Use had in the flashback: he had trained, she had practised.
items.explanation: A flashback interrupts the main story to show an earlier event. It helps the reader understand why the present moment matters to the character.

items.prompt: Write a persuasive article for your school magazine arguing that every class should have one lesson a week outdoors. Use at least three persuasive techniques.

criteria.label: States a clear viewpoint at the start
Gives at least three reasons with evidence
Uses persuasive techniques such as rhetorical questions and emotive language
Answers an opposing view
Ends with a strong conclusion or call to action
Spelling, grammar and punctuation are accurate

planning: What is your main argument, in one sentence?
Which three reasons are strongest, and what evidence supports each one?
Which techniques will you use: rhetorical questions, facts, emotive words?
How will you answer people who disagree?
What will your final sentence be?
items.model:
Learning Under the Sky

How much of your school day do you spend looking at four walls? For most of us, the answer is almost all of it. It is time for every class to have one lesson a week outdoors.

First, outdoor lessons bring learning to life. Measuring the shadow of a tree teaches angles better than any diagram.

Secondly, after lessons outside, many pupils say they feel calmer and more ready to work.

Some teachers worry about rain or noise. However, our school has a covered terrace and a quiet garden that are empty most mornings.

One lesson a week costs nothing and needs no new equipment. Let us take our learning outside.
hints: Open with a question or a surprising fact to hook your reader.
Think about what a teacher might worry about, and answer that worry.
items.explanation: A persuasive article states a clear view, supports it with reasons and evidence, answers objections and ends with a call to action.

items.prompt: Which of these is a feature of a formal letter?

options.text: Yours faithfully,
See ya!
options.why: This is an informal way to end a message.

options.text: Once upon a time
options.why: This is a story opening.

options.text: Ingredients:
options.why: This is a heading in a recipe.

hints: Think about how a formal letter ends.
Formal letters use polite, set phrases.
Cross out the options that belong to stories, recipes and chats.
items.explanation: Yours faithfully is a formal sign-off, used when the letter begins Dear Sir or Madam.

items.prompt: Which sentence would best open a balanced argument?

options.text: Should pupils wear school uniform? There are strong views on both sides.
School uniform is the worst idea ever invented!
options.why: This is one-sided and informal, so it does not suit a balanced argument.

options.text: Once upon a time, a boy lost his school tie.
options.why: This is a story opening.

options.text: Buy your uniform at our shop today!
options.why: This is an advert.

hints: A balanced argument looks at both sides of a question.
Its opening usually introduces the question without taking a side.
Find the opening that mentions both sides.
items.explanation: A balanced argument begins by introducing the question and showing that there are different views.

items.prompt: Put the parts of a news report in order.
items: Opening paragraph: who, what, where and when
hints: Think about the front page of a newspaper.
The most important information comes first, and details come later.
Start with the large words at the very top.
items.explanation: A news report starts with a headline and the reporter’s name. The opening paragraph gives the key facts, then come details and quotations, and the end looks ahead.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a flashback?

options.text: Mira walked onto the stage and began to dance.
options.why: This happens in the present of the story.

options.text: Tomorrow, Mira will dance on the stage.
options.why: This looks forward to the future.

options.text: As she waited on the stage, Mira remembered the day her grandmother had first taught her to dance.
Mira danced, and the audience clapped loudly.
options.why: This tells events in order, with no jump back.

hints: A flashback takes the reader back to an earlier time.
Look for words such as remembered and had.
Find the sentence that moves from the present to the past.
items.explanation: Remembered and had first taught take the reader back to an earlier event, so this sentence uses a flashback.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a persuasive text?

options.text: to make the reader agree with the writer’s view
to tell a story with characters
options.why: A story entertains. A persuasive text argues a view.

options.text: to list facts about a place
options.why: That describes an information text.

options.text: to give steps for making something
options.why: That describes instructions.

hints: Think about the word persuade.
Persuade means to make someone believe or do something.
Find the purpose that is about changing the reader’s mind.
items.explanation: A persuasive text tries to convince the reader to agree or act.

items.prompt: Sort the features by the type of writing they belong to.

items.text: The sender’s address at the top

hints: A formal letter is written to an organisation or official.
A story has characters and a plot.
Start with Yours faithfully. Which text ends this way?
items.explanation: Yours faithfully, Dear Sir or Madam and an address belong to formal letters. Once upon a time, dialogue and a plot with a problem belong to stories.

items.prompt: Put the parts of a persuasive article in order.
hints: A title comes first.
State your view before the reasons.
The call to action finishes the text.
items.explanation: A persuasive article has a title, a clear opening view, reasons with evidence, an answer to the other side and a call to action.

items.prompt: Build a persuasive opinion sentence. Use the cards.
items.answer: In my opinion, schools should start later.
hints: Persuasive writing often begins with a phrase that gives an opinion.
The phrase has three words and a comma.
Schools is the subject, should start is the verb.
items.explanation: In my opinion, is an opinion phrase. The sentence then follows normal order: subject, verb, and a time word.

items.prompt: Which opening sentence is best for a news report?

options.text: I think fires are very scary.
options.why: News reports give facts, not personal feelings.

options.text: Once there was a market full of fruit.
options.why: This is a story opening.

options.text: Yesterday, a fire at a market in Solo destroyed ten stalls, but nobody was hurt.
Do you like markets?
options.why: A news report states facts and does not begin with a question.

hints: A news report tells the reader what happened.
It answers who, what, where and when.
Look for the sentence with facts and a time.
items.explanation: A news report opens with the main facts: what happened, where and when.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the best conclusion for a balanced argument about school uniforms?

options.text: Uniforms are the worst idea ever.
options.why: A balanced argument does not take an extreme view.

options.text: Overall, uniforms bring equality, but pupils should also have some choice, so a flexible rule may be best.
I like blue.
options.why: This does not weigh the points.

options.text: Many schools have uniforms.
options.why: This only states a fact and does not give a judgement.

hints: A balanced argument looks at both sides.
The conclusion weighs the points and gives a final view.
Look for the answer that mentions both sides.
items.explanation: A balanced conclusion weighs both sides and gives a fair judgement.

items.prompt: Name the text type. It explains how something works, with sub-headings and diagrams. Write recount, report or explanation.
hints: Think about the purpose: to explain how or why something happens.
A recount tells events in order. A report describes facts about a topic.
Which type explains a process?
items.explanation: An explanation text explains how or why something happens, often with sub-headings and diagrams.

items.prompt: Choose all the features of a biography.

options.text: It is written in the past tense.
It uses made-up characters.
options.why: A biography is about a real person.

options.text: It often includes dates.
It tells events from a real person’s life in time order.
It is written as a first-person diary.
options.why: That describes an autobiography or a diary.

hints: A biography is the story of someone’s life.
Think about the tense, the person and the order of events.
Check which features are about real events.
items.explanation: A biography is about a real person, written in the past tense and in time order, usually with dates.

items.prompt: You are writing about the water cycle for Year 2 pupils. Which sentence suits your audience best?

options.text: The sun heats the water and it rises into the sky like a tiny hidden cloud.
Evaporation occurs when thermal energy converts liquid into vapour.
options.why: Too technical for Year 2.

options.text: Water goes up.
options.why: Too short and unclear.

options.text: Hydrological circulation transfers moisture.
options.why: Too advanced for young readers.

hints: Think about who will read the text.
Young readers need simple words and pictures in words.
Choose the sentence that is clear but interesting.
items.explanation: Writers adapt vocabulary for their audience. This sentence is simple, clear and interesting for young readers.

items.prompt: Put the parts of this story in order. It uses a flashback.
items: Wulan stood at the start line, her heart pounding.
She remembered the cold mornings when she practised alone.
The whistle blew, and she was back in the present.
She sprinted past the others on the final bend.
She crossed the line and smiled at her coach.
hints: Find the sentence that starts the scene.
The flashback tells about the past, then the story returns to now.
The ending is the last event.
items.explanation: The story opens at the start line, flashes back to practice, returns with the whistle, builds to the race and ends with the finish.

items.prompt: Which sentence best uses persuasive techniques for a leaflet to stop litter?

options.text: Litter is on the ground in many places.
options.why: This states a fact only and does not persuade.

options.text: Do you want a clean, beautiful park? Then pick up your rubbish today!
I do not like litter.
options.why: This is a personal opinion with no technique.

options.text: The park has trees and benches.
options.why: This is a description, not persuasion.

hints: Persuasive techniques include questions to the reader and commands.
Look for a sentence that speaks to the reader directly.
Check for an appeal and a call to action.
items.explanation: The rhetorical question and the command speak to the reader and ask for action.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences into fact and opinion for a balanced argument.

items.text: Jakarta has over ten million people.
The city is the best place to live.
The Monas tower is 132 metres tall.

hints: A fact can be checked.
An opinion shows what someone thinks or feels.
Ask: can I prove this is true?
items.explanation: Facts such as heights and numbers can be checked. Words like best, boring and better show opinions.

items.prompt: Read: Mobile phones are terrible. They ruin everything and nobody should ever have one. Why does this paragraph not suit a balanced argument?

options.text: It uses too many long words.
options.why: The words are simple. The problem is the content.

options.text: It has no verbs.
options.why: The sentences contain verbs.

options.text: It is too polite.
options.why: The tone is not polite. It is extreme.

options.text: It gives only one extreme view and no evidence.

hints: A balanced argument considers both sides.
Look at the words terrible, ruin and nobody.
Check whether evidence is given.
items.explanation: A balanced argument weighs both sides with evidence. This paragraph is one-sided and exaggerated.

items.prompt: You are writing a letter to the mayor asking for a new library. Which extract matches both purpose and audience?

options.text: I am writing to request a library in our neighbourhood. A library would give children a quiet place to read and study.
Hey Mayor! We need a library, it would be awesome!
options.why: Too casual for a formal letter.

options.text: Libraries have books, and books are made of paper.
options.why: This states a fact that does not support the request.

options.text: You have to build a library or I will be angry.
options.why: This is rude and does not persuade.

hints: Think about who will read the letter and why you are writing.
A formal letter is polite and gives reasons.
Pick the extract that states the purpose and a reason.
items.explanation: The extract is formal, states the purpose clearly and gives a reason, so it suits a letter to the mayor.

items.prompt: Which shows the correct layout of a playscript?

options.text: Maya said, "Is anyone there?" and she opened the door.
options.why: This is a story, not a playscript.

options.text: MAYA: (opening the door) Is anyone there?
"Is anyone there?" Maya asked.
options.why: Playscripts do not use speech marks.

options.text: Maya - opens door - is anyone there.
options.why: This is not set out as a script.

hints: Playscripts put the speaker's name at the start.
Stage directions go in brackets.
Look for a name, a colon and then the words.
items.explanation: A playscript starts with the character's name, then any stage direction in brackets, then the words to be spoken.

items.prompt: Which stage direction best shows that the character is nervous?

options.text: (smiling widely)
options.why: This shows happiness.

options.text: (sitting down)
options.why: This is plain and does not show feeling.

options.text: (glancing at the door, twisting a button)
(eating lunch)
options.why: This does not show nerves.

hints: Stage directions show feelings through actions.
What do nervous people do with their hands and eyes?
Look for small movements.
items.explanation: Glancing at the door and twisting a button show nerves through action.

items.prompt: Which sentence best signals a flashback in a story?

options.text: Suddenly the door opened.
options.why: This is a new event in the present.

options.text: Next day, Ayu went to school.
options.why: This moves forward in time.

options.text: Meanwhile, the cat slept.
options.why: This is a different place at the same time.

options.text: Years earlier, in her grandmother's kitchen, Ayu had first tasted the soup.

hints: A flashback goes back in time.
Look for a phrase about an earlier time.
Which sentence uses had and years earlier?
items.explanation: Years earlier and the past perfect had tasted take the reader back to an earlier time, a flashback.

items.prompt: The same football match is told twice. Which version gives the goalkeeper's viewpoint?

options.text: The striker ran, kicked and the crowd cheered as the ball flew.
options.why: This describes the match from outside, mostly about the striker.

options.text: The referee blew the whistle and the game began.
options.why: This is an outside view.

options.text: I saw the ball leave the striker's boot and my stomach dropped as I dived.
The crowd waved flags in the afternoon sun.
options.why: This is the crowd's view, not the goalkeeper's.

hints: Viewpoint means whose eyes we see through.
Look for I and feelings.
The goalkeeper dives and feels the shot.
items.explanation: Using I, the writer shows what the goalkeeper sees and feels, so this gives the goalkeeper's viewpoint.

items.prompt: Which sentence builds a setting using several senses?

options.text: It was a place.
options.why: This gives no detail.

options.text: The room was big.
options.why: This gives size only.

options.text: Smoke from the grill stung my eyes, and the clatter of plates rang above the chatter.
The market is in the city.
options.why: This tells where, not what it feels like.

hints: Senses include sight, sound, smell and touch.
Which sentence lets you feel like you are there?
Look for stung and clatter.
items.explanation: The sentence uses sight, smell and sound to bring the setting to life.

items.prompt: When should you use a numbered list instead of bullet points?

options.text: When the items are in no particular order
options.why: Bullets are better for unordered items.

options.text: When the steps must be done in order
When there is only one item
options.why: A list needs at least two items.

options.text: When you want to decorate the page
options.why: Lists should help the reader, not decorate.

hints: Numbers show order.
Think of a recipe.
Bullets are for things that can be read in any order.
items.explanation: Numbers show a fixed order, such as steps. Bullet points are for items in any order.

items.prompt: Sort each item by the kind of list it suits.

items.text: Steps to set up a tent

hints: Does the order matter?
Steps need numbers.
Start with Steps to set up a tent.
items.explanation: Steps and directions must be followed in order, so they need numbers. Packing items and features can be read in any order.

items.prompt: Which bulleted list is written consistently?

options.text: Pack a torch / A water bottle / Taking snacks
options.why: The items start in different ways.

options.text: Pack a torch / Bring a water bottle / Snacks too
options.why: The last item does not match the first two.

options.text: Pack a torch / Bring a water bottle / Take some snacks
A torch / Bring water / Snacks to eat
options.why: The items start in different ways.

hints: In a good list each item has the same pattern.
Look at the first word of each item.
Choose the list where every line starts with a command.
items.explanation: Every item begins with a verb command, so the list is parallel and easy to read.

items.prompt: Which layout suits a poster for the school fair that people read from far away?

options.text: Small writing in long paragraphs
options.why: This is hard to read from far away.

options.text: A large heading, a few short lines and a big picture
Only a picture with no words
options.why: Readers need to know the date and place.

options.text: A long list of rules in tiny print
options.why: Tiny print is hard to read quickly.

hints: A poster must be read quickly.
Big and short is best.
Which choice has large letters?
items.explanation: A poster uses a large heading, short text and a picture so readers get the message quickly.

items.prompt: Which feature best suits an onscreen presentation?

options.text: Full paragraphs copied from a book
options.why: Too much text is hard to read on a screen.

options.text: Short bullet points in a large, clear font
A tiny font to fit more words
options.why: Small text cannot be read from the back.

options.text: No pictures or headings
options.why: Headings and pictures help the audience.

hints: People read slides from a distance.
Think of big, short and clear.
Which choice has short lines?
items.explanation: On screen, short points in a large font are easy to read at a distance.

items.prompt: Rangga listens to a talk about bats and wants to write notes. Which is best?

options.text: Write every word the speaker says
options.why: This is too slow and hard to read later.

options.text: Write key words and short phrases such as nocturnal, eat insects, use echoes
Write only the title
options.why: This is too little to help.

options.text: Draw a picture of a bat
options.why: A picture alone will not hold the facts.

hints: Notes should be quick and short.
Use key words instead of whole sentences.
Choose the notes that you can read back easily.
items.explanation: Good notes use key words and short phrases so you can write quickly and still remember the facts.

items.prompt: Choose all the times when it is helpful to take notes.

options.text: Researching a topic from several books
Watching a funny film with friends
options.why: You are watching for fun and do not need to remember details.

options.text: Listening to a talk before writing a report
Eating lunch
options.why: There is nothing to record.

hints: Notes help you remember facts for later.
When will you need to use the information?
Which activities involve learning facts for a task?
items.explanation: Notes help when you collect facts to use later, such as for research or a report.
